content: The findings indicate that all handwashing methods were generally effective in practice. However, two key observations were made: (1) Calcium hypochlorite (HTH) was consistently safer and more effective compared to other methods; and (2) chlorine-based solutions, when compared to soap and water or hand sanitizers, provided the added benefit of reducing pathogen persistence in rinsing water. While each handwashing method has its own advantages and limitations, it is recommended that Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) responders and communities adopt the method(s) that are most acceptable, available, and feasible. Chlorine solutions, in particular, may help reduce transmission risks associated with contaminated rinsing water. Across various simulations, HTH performed exceptionally well. Chlorine solutions prepared from HTH demonstrated the longest shelf life, caused the least hand irritation, and achieved the highest handwashing efficacy. However, HTH presents operational challenges, such as being more explosive than sodium dichloroisocyanurate (NaDCC) and forming precipitates during mixing that can clog pipes. In well-maintained Ebola Treatment Units (ETUs), these issues can be managed with proper training and maintenance. Nevertheless, during the West African outbreak, explosions occurred in ETUs managed by less experienced organizations, posing significant risks to the health and safety of both response personnel and patients. Reidy et al. (2017) conducted an expert review of personal protective equipment (PPE) solutions for UK military medical personnel working in an ETU in Sierra Leone. They emphasized the importance of maintaining tactility and dexterity through the use of two pairs of gloves, selecting 400-mm nitrile, powder-free gloves. Competency in PPE use was developed through a nine-day pre-deployment training program, which allowed over 60 clinical personnel per deployment to practice PPE skills in simulated ETUs and classrooms. The training provided evidence-based PPE solutions, skills in donning and doffing PPE, confidence in the selected PPE, and testing of individuals’ ability to safely perform tasks while wearing PPE. Gao et al. (2016) conducted laboratory testing on gloves following US CDC guidance for disinfecting gloved hands during PPE removal after caring for Ebola patients. The guidance recommends multiple applications of alcohol-based hand rubs (ABHR) on medical exam gloves. The study evaluated the effects of ABHR on the integrity of 13 brands of nitrile and latex gloves from five manufacturers, using two different ABHR formulations. The tensile strength of gloves generally decreased with each ABHR application. Nitrile gloves were more affected than latex gloves, and ethanol-based ABHR caused less reduction in tensile strength compared to isopropanol-based ABHR. The investigators recommended that hospital staff practice using ABHR and doffing gloves to become familiar with changes in glove properties. No studies were found that examined the effects of disinfecting outer gloves with alcohol-based hand rubs or chlorine solutions. Similarly, no evidence was found on the psychological effects (e.g., stigma) associated with spraying homes with disinfectants or patient experiences. Regarding environmental cleaning and disinfection, no studies compared the efficacy of wiping versus spraying disinfectants. However, wiping was found to reduce contamination levels on surfaces through mechanical action, even without disinfectants. Chlorine-based solutions, particularly at 0. Pre-cleaning practices, such as wiping or covering, did not significantly increase disinfection efficacy but could limit splashing. For heavily soiled linens resulting from EVD or Marburg disease care, no studies met eligibility criteria to compare disinfection versus elimination methods. Waste management during outbreaks remains a significant challenge.
